title: The War That May Have Happened
summary: Whether the Trojan War happened is one of the most debated questions in ancient history. Hittite texts from the 13th century BC mention 'Wilusa' — almost certainly Ilios, the Greek name for Troy — and record a military dispute involving the city. Heinrich Schliemann excavated Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey from 1871, finding a city destroyed by fire in the right era that he identified as Troy. Modern archaeologists have confirmed that a significant settlement called Troy VIIa was indeed destroyed around 1180-1150 BC, at the right time and in the right circumstances for it to be the historical kernel of the legend. The scale of the events that Homer describes is certainly mythologised — but the memory of a Greek military expedition to the Anatolian coast almost certainly preserves something real.

title: The World Ends — Writing Disappears
summary: Around 1200 BC, the Bronze Age civilisations of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed with extraordinary rapidity. The Mycenaean palaces of Greece were burned and abandoned; the Hittite Empire disintegrated; the Egyptian New Kingdom struggled to survive; the great trading cities of the Syrian coast were destroyed. The agents of this collapse — conventionally called the 'Sea Peoples' — are still debated. Within a generation, the Linear B script that Mycenaean Greeks had used for administrative records disappeared entirely: there was no longer any palace bureaucracy to use it, no scribes to learn it, and no cultural continuity to preserve it. Greece entered a four-century Dark Age. The only vessel in which the memory of the Mycenaean world survived was the oral tradition — the songs the bards sang at aristocratic feasts.

title: The Bards Remember
summary: For four centuries after the Bronze Age collapse, Greek culture had no writing. The memory of the Mycenaean world — its heroes, its wars, its gods, its lost palaces — survived entirely in oral performance. Travelling bards called aoidoi performed at aristocratic feasts, singing of Achilles and Odysseus and the war at Troy for audiences who had never seen Linear B and could not have read it if they had. The oral tradition was not the same as memorisation: bards did not recite fixed texts from memory but composed afresh in performance, using a repertoire of formulaic phrases — 'wine-dark sea,' 'swift-footed Achilles,' 'rosy-fingered Dawn' — that could be combined in metrical lines. Each performance was unique; the stories were stable. The poems we call Homer's were being assembled, line by line, for centuries before anyone thought to write them down.

title: Writing Returns to Greece
summary: Around 800 BC, the Greeks adapted the Phoenician alphabet — adding vowels that Semitic scripts lacked — to create the first fully phonetic writing system in human history. Every sound in spoken Greek could now be represented in writing; every written Greek text could be read aloud by anyone who knew the alphabet. The new script spread rapidly across the Greek world. For the first time since the Bronze Age collapse, thoughts could be preserved outside human memory. The oral tradition that had kept Greek culture alive through four centuries of illiteracy now faced a transformative choice: its greatest achievements could be written down. Someone — or many someones — decided to write down the poems about Troy.

title: Homer Puts Down the Lyre
summary: Around 750-700 BC, the poems we know as the Iliad and the Odyssey were written down for the first time. The Iliad — 15,693 lines of verse describing 51 days in the final year of the Trojan War — and the Odyssey — 12,109 lines following Odysseus' ten-year journey home — together constitute the oldest and most influential works of Western literature. Who wrote them down, and in what circumstances, is unknown. 'Homer' is the name attached to both poems by ancient tradition, but ancient authorities already disagreed about who he was: whether he was one person or two, whether he was blind, which city he came from. Seven cities claimed to be his birthplace. The poems themselves contain no autobiographical information. The most celebrated author in Western literature may be a name attached to a tradition rather than a description of a person.

title: Who Was Homer?
summary: The 'Homeric Question' — who wrote the Iliad and Odyssey, and were they the work of one poet or many — is one of the longest-running debates in literary scholarship. Ancient commentators already noticed inconsistencies between the two poems and within them; some argued for two different Homers, others for one. In the 18th century, the German scholar Friedrich Wolf published Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795), arguing systematically that the poems could not be the work of a single author and must have been assembled from multiple shorter poems. The debate intensified through the 19th and 20th centuries. It was not resolved by argument but by fieldwork — a Harvard scholar who went to Yugoslavia and listened to living bards.

title: The Tyrant Fixes the Text
summary: Ancient tradition — reported by Cicero and later sources, though not by any contemporary 6th-century witness — holds that the Athenian tyrant Peisistratos ordered the Homeric poems collected and performed at the Panathenaic festival in a fixed order and from a standardised text. Modern scholars treat this 'Peisistratean recension' with real skepticism: the story may exaggerate or invent a more dramatic single moment of standardisation than what was probably a gradual process across many decades and rhapsodes. What is not in serious doubt is the outcome, whoever was responsible for it: by the mid-6th century BC, a broadly standard version of the poems existed and was performed publicly in Athens, suppressing whatever variant regional versions had existed. The standardisation was politically convenient for Athens either way — it let the city claim to present the definitive Homer — and it was historically consequential: by fixing the text, someone preserved it.

title: Every Greek Child Learns Homer
summary: Homer became the foundation of Greek education in the classical period. Children learned to read using Homer; students memorised long passages; teachers used the poems as the source of examples in grammar, rhetoric, ethics, and theology. The Athenian comic playwright Aristophanes could assume his audience knew large sections of Homer by heart; philosophers referenced him constantly — whether to use his authority or argue against it. When Plato, in the Republic, proposed banning poets from his ideal city, he was primarily arguing against Homer, whose portrayal of the gods he considered morally dangerous. The poems were so central to Greek culture that attacking poetry meant attacking Homer. Alexander the Great, educated by Aristotle, slept with an annotated copy of the Iliad under his pillow.

title: Alexandria Collects and Edits Homer
summary: The Library of Alexandria made Homer one of its primary scholarly projects. The librarians Zenodotus, Aristophanes of Byzantium, and Aristarchus of Samothrace collected every manuscript of the Iliad and Odyssey they could find, compared variant readings, and produced critical editions that attempted to establish the most authoritative text. Aristarchus' commentary on Homer — which occupied multiple volumes — was the most sophisticated piece of literary scholarship produced in the ancient world. The Alexandrian text became the standard version; later manuscripts descend from it. Without Alexandria, the textual tradition would have fragmented into incompatible versions. The library that preserved Euclid and Archimedes also preserved the poems that had taught Greeks to read for five centuries.

title: Alexander and Achilles
summary: Alexander the Great carried an annotated copy of the Iliad — prepared by his teacher Aristotle — on all his campaigns. He considered Achilles his personal hero and role model: when he reached the Troad at the beginning of his Asian campaign, he visited the tomb traditionally identified as Achilles' and laid a wreath on it, declaring himself fortunate to have Homer as the herald of his virtue. The identification was not merely sentimental: Alexander's conquests spread the Greek language and Homeric culture across an arc from Egypt to the borders of India, creating the Hellenistic world in which Homer was studied from Alexandria to Bactria. The poems that had shaped Alexander had, through Alexander, shaped the world that preserved them.

title: Virgil Writes Rome's Homer
summary: Virgil's Aeneid (written 29-19 BC, published posthumously) was the most deliberate act of literary response in antiquity: a Roman epic built on the structural model of both Homeric poems, following Aeneas from the fall of Troy to the founding of Rome, and establishing for Roman culture the same foundational mythological role that Homer served for Greek culture. The Aeneid begins in the middle of the action (like the Odyssey), moves to a war narrative (like the Iliad), and deliberately echoes Homeric formulas in Latin. Educated Romans read Homer in Greek from childhood; educated Romans' children read Virgil. Through Virgil, the Homeric structure became the template for epic poetry in Latin — and through Latin, for the entire European literary tradition.

title: Byzantine Scholars Keep the Flame
summary: The survival of Homer through the collapse of the Western Roman Empire is largely the achievement of Byzantine scholarship. While Latin literacy declined in Western Europe, Greek continued to be read in Constantinople, and the Byzantine educational system kept Homer at its centre: students continued to memorise passages from the Iliad and Odyssey, commentators continued to write on the poems, and copyists produced new manuscripts across a thousand years of Byzantine history. When Italian humanists of the 14th and 15th centuries began recovering Greek texts, Byzantine scholars were their primary teachers and sources. Without Byzantine preservation, the Homeric poems might have survived only in fragments, as so much ancient literature did. Every medieval manuscript of the Iliad and Odyssey that survives today — hundreds of them, along with even more fragmentary papyri from antiquity — descends from the Byzantine copying tradition.

title: Dante Meets a Poet He Cannot Read
summary: Dante Alighieri, writing the Divine Comedy around 1308-1320, placed Homer first among the great poets in Limbo — the dwelling place of virtuous pagans who died before Christianity. 'That is Homer, sovereign poet,' Virgil tells Dante, who bows in respect. The irony is that Dante almost certainly could not read Greek and had never read Homer directly. He knew the Trojan story through Latin summaries and Virgil's Aeneid. Homer was, for Dante, a name and a reputation rather than a text — the founding figure of a tradition he knew only through intermediaries. The scene in the Inferno captures perfectly how Homer had survived: not always read, but always present, the invisible origin of everything that came after.

title: Every Story in the Shadow of Troy
summary: The Iliad and Odyssey stand at the origin of Western literature not merely chronologically but structurally: the hero's journey, the homecoming, the catalogue of the dead, the descent into the underworld, the test of identity, the loyal spouse, the clever villain — these narrative templates were established in Homer and have been repeated, varied, and subverted in every subsequent literary tradition. Milton wrote Paradise Lost in conscious dialogue with Homer. Alexander Pope's translations made Homer available to 18th-century England; Keats wrote a sonnet on first reading Chapman's Homer. The structure of the Odyssey underlies Joyce's Ulysses, Walcott's Omeros, Atwood's Penelopiad. The poems were composed without writing, by an unknown figure, from the fragments of a Bronze Age war. They have generated more literature than any other texts in human history.

title: Ulysses — Homer in Dublin
summary: James Joyce's Ulysses, published on February 2, 1922 — Joyce's fortieth birthday — is structured as a chapter-by-chapter parallel to the Odyssey, following Leopold Bloom through a single day in Dublin on June 16, 1904. Bloom is Odysseus; his wife Molly is Penelope; Stephen Dedalus is Telemachus. The correspondence is detailed, ironic, and sometimes deliberately hidden — Joyce gave each chapter a Homeric title that he then suppressed from the published text. The novel is widely considered one of the greatest works of fiction in the English language. That the Odyssey — composed orally in archaic Greek, written down in the 8th century BC, preserved through Alexandrian scholarship and Byzantine copying — could generate, three thousand years later, a novel set in a Dublin pub in 1904, is perhaps the most eloquent testimony to what oral tradition can produce when it finally finds paper.

title: The Man Who Went to Yugoslavia to Find Homer
summary: Milman Parry was a Harvard classicist who, in the late 1920s, developed the theory that the Iliad and Odyssey had been composed through an oral-formulaic technique — that the repeated phrases ('wine-dark sea,' 'swift-footed Achilles') were not decorative but structural, serving as building blocks that allowed a bard to compose thousands of lines of metrically perfect verse in live performance. To test this theory, he went to Yugoslavia in 1933-35 with a recording machine and documented the guslari — South Slavic oral epic singers who still composed in the same way. He found that living illiterate bards could produce and perform poems of Homeric length and complexity, composed fresh at each performance using the same formulaic techniques. Homer had not been a singular genius but a tradition. Parry died in 1935 aged 33, in circumstances suggesting either suicide or accident. His student Albert Lord published The Singer of Tales in 1960, completing the argument.

title: The Poems Are More Extraordinary Than We Thought
summary: Milman Parry and Albert Lord's oral-formulaic theory, confirmed through fieldwork among Yugoslav guslars and accepted by the scholarly community from the 1960s onward, transformed the understanding of what the Iliad and Odyssey are. They are not the work of a single blind genius sitting down to write — they are the crystallisation of four centuries of oral tradition, the accumulated work of generations of bards who sang about the Trojan War at aristocratic feasts through the Greek Dark Ages. Homer, if he existed, was the last great singer who happened to be recorded — the point at which a living tradition became a frozen text. The poems are not diminished by this understanding; they are enlarged by it. What survives is not one man's imagination but an entire civilisation's memory, shaped by four hundred years of performance into the most influential poems in the history of human literature.

title: Troy Without Homer
summary: For roughly eight centuries, almost no one in Western Europe could read Homer. Greek literacy had nearly vanished after the fall of Rome, and the actual text of the Iliad and Odyssey was effectively inaccessible to Latin readers. Yet the story of Troy remained one of the most popular narratives in medieval literature — transmitted through two short Latin prose texts, 'De Excidio Troiae' attributed to 'Dares Phrygius' and 'Ephemeris Belli Troiani' attributed to 'Dictys Cretensis,' both probably composed in the 4th–6th centuries AD and claiming, falsely, to be eyewitness accounts more reliable than Homer's supposedly fanciful epic. Medieval writers overwhelmingly preferred these forgeries to Homer precisely because Homer was unavailable and unreadable — and because the pseudo-eyewitness framing suited an audience uninterested in poetic invention. Benoît de Sainte-Maure's 'Roman de Troie' (c. 1165) and Guido delle Colonne's 'Historia Destructionis Troiae' (1287), both based on Dares and Dictys rather than Homer, were the source for Chaucer's Troilus and Criseyde and, ultimately, for Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida. Europe told the story of Troy for eight hundred years using texts that were not just inferior to Homer but invented to replace him.

title: Schliemann Digs Through Homer's Troy to Find It
summary: Heinrich Schliemann, a self-made German businessman with no formal archaeological training and an unshakeable literal faith in the Iliad, began excavating the mound of Hisarlik in northwestern Turkey in 1871, convinced it concealed Homer's Troy. He was largely right about the location — but his methods were catastrophic. Digging a vast trench straight through the mound in search of what he assumed would be the grandest layer, Schliemann's crews demolished significant portions of Troy VIIa, the layer now considered the strongest candidate for the historical Troy of the Trojan War, in their haste to reach the more dramatic Bronze Age fortifications beneath it. In 1873 he uncovered a hoard of gold jewellery and artefacts he called 'Priam's Treasure,' smuggled it out of Ottoman territory, and photographed his wife Sophia wearing the jewels — a publicity coup that made Schliemann internationally famous and archaeology internationally scandalous. The treasure was seized by the Red Army from Berlin in 1945 and vanished for nearly fifty years before resurfacing in Moscow's Pushkin Museum in 1993. Schliemann had proved that Homer's Troy was, in some sense, real — while destroying irreplaceable evidence about exactly what that reality had been.
